name: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications
aliases: Microvascular and macrovascular complications of diabetes

clinicalPearls: Diabetes-related complications are split into vascular (microvascular: retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy; macrovascular: coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure) and nonvascular (infections, dermatologic changes, cheiroarthropathy, hearing loss, cataracts, glaucoma, fractures, cognitive impairment); patterns are similar in type 1 and type 2 disease.

Microvascular complications generally do not become evident until the second decade of hyperglycemia, whereas atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk (driven by insulin resistance and dyslipidemia) may precede frank hyperglycemia, so type 2 patients often have complications already present at diagnosis.

Landmark trials established that chronic hyperglycemia is causative for microvascular disease: in the DCCT, intensive control (HbA1c 7.3% vs 9.1%) reduced retinopathy ~47%, albuminuria ~39%, clinical nephropathy ~54%, and neuropathy ~60%; the UKPDS showed each 1-percentage-point HbA1c reduction lowered microvascular complications by about 35%.

A 'metabolic memory' / legacy effect exists: a period of improved glycemic control yields reduced cardiovascular events and mortality more than a decade later even after glycemic separation between groups disappears (DCCT/EDIC showed ~57% fewer cardiovascular events and ~33% lower mortality long term).

Diabetic retinopathy is staged as nonproliferative (microaneurysms, blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous caliber change, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities) and proliferative (neovascularization from retinal hypoxemia, risking vitreous hemorrhage and traction retinal detachment); neovascularization is the hallmark of the proliferative stage.

Macular edema can occur at either retinopathy stage and is a key cause of moderate vision loss; duration of diabetes and degree of glycemic control are the strongest predictors of retinopathy, with hypertension, nephropathy, and dyslipidemia as additional risk factors.

Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease and stage 5 CKD; screening combines a spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and estimated GFR because some patients lose GFR without albuminuria. Albuminuria is a persistently increased UACR >30 mg/g (moderate 30-299 mg/g, severe >300 mg/g).

Diabetic neuropathy affects roughly half of long-standing patients and includes distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN), autonomic neuropathy, and mononeuropathy/radiculopathy; up to 50% of those with DSPN are asymptomatic, so screening for loss of protective sensation (10-g monofilament, vibration) is essential.

Cardiovascular disease (CHD, PAD, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure) is the major cause of death in diabetes; heart failure is about twice as common (HFpEF, HFmrEF, or HFrEF) and 'silent ischemia' with absent chest pain is frequent, warranting a cardiac evaluation before major surgery.

Diabetes is the leading cause of nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation; foot ulcers arise from the interaction of neuropathy, abnormal biomechanics, peripheral arterial disease, and poor wound healing, and a wound that probes to bone is highly likely to harbor osteomyelitis.

Patients have greater frequency and severity of infections; certain severe infections occur almost exclusively in diabetes: rhinocerebral mucormycosis, emphysematous cholecystitis/pyelonephritis/cystitis, and malignant (invasive) otitis externa (usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa).

Characteristic dermatologic findings include xerosis/pruritus, diabetic dermopathy (pigmented pretibial papules), bullosis diabeticorum, necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum (predominantly young women), acanthosis nigricans (severe insulin resistance), and vitiligo/alopecia areata in type 1 disease.
harrison.pathophysiology: Chronic hyperglycemia is the principal etiologic driver of microvascular complications, though the precise mechanisms remain incompletely defined and are likely multifactorial. Proposed pathways include hyperglycemia-induced epigenetic changes altering gene expression, formation of advanced glycosylation end products (e.g., pentosidine, glucosepane, carboxymethyllysine) that cross-link proteins and bind cell-surface receptors causing endothelial and glomerular dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis, local growth-factor effects (VEGF-A drives proliferative retinopathy), and a unifying hypothesis that hyperglycemia raises mitochondrial reactive oxygen species/superoxide that activate downstream injury pathways. In nephropathy, soluble mediators (angiotensin II, endothelin, AGEs), hemodynamic alterations (glomerular hyperfiltration, increased capillary pressure), and structural changes (basement-membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, fibrosis) lead from early hyperfiltration/renal hypertrophy to irreversible albuminuria and GFR decline. Macrovascular disease additionally reflects insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and inflammation, with insulin failing to suppress adipose lipolysis and causing ectopic lipid accumulation (triglycerides, diacylglycerol, ceramides). In neuropathy both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers are lost; foot ulceration arises from sensory loss removing protective mechanisms, autonomic anhidrosis causing dry/fissured skin, motor changes producing deformity, and PAD impairing healing.
additionalDifferentials: Diabetic neuropathy is a diagnosis of exclusion - confirm only after excluding other neuropathy causes (e.g., B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, other metabolic/toxic neuropathies)
Chronic kidney disease without retinopathy in type 1 diabetes should prompt investigation for an alternative (non-diabetic) cause of renal disease
Type IV renal tubular acidosis (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism) as a cause of hyperkalemia/acidemia in diabetic patients
Renovascular hypertension when blood pressure is not readily controlled in type 2 diabetes
Celiac disease in type 1 diabetes presenting with diarrhea/constipation (associated anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies)
Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, possibly autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome) in type 1 diabetes with orthostatic hypotension
infectionMimics: Gas gangrene appearance in a diabetic foot may develop in the absence of clostridial infection
Superficial culture of any foot ulcer yields multiple bacterial species of uncertain significance - infected ulcer is a clinical diagnosis, not a culture diagnosis
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common with diabetic cystopathy and generally does not require treatment
nonInfectiousMimics: Transient worsening of established retinopathy during the first 6-12 months of improved glycemic control (and with GLP-1 receptor agonist-associated rapid glycemic improvement) can mimic disease progression but is temporary

UACR can be falsely elevated by strenuous exercise, fever, infection, congestive heart failure, marked hyperglycemia, marked hypertension, or prostate disease - confirm on 2-3 occasions over 3-6 months
Acute painful diabetic neuropathy may be treatment-related, triggered by improved glycemic control
additionalInvestigations: Dilated retinal examination by optometrist/ophthalmologist or retinal photography with remote reading (nondilated primary-care exams are inadequate); fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography to detect macular edema
Spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) plus estimated GFR, screening annually (start 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, at diagnosis for type 2)
Annual neuropathy screening with 10-g monofilament and vibration testing to detect loss of protective sensation; begin 5 years after type 1 diagnosis and at diagnosis of type 2
Gastric scintigraphy after a radiolabeled meal to document delayed gastric emptying (may not correlate with symptoms) in suspected gastroparesis
Ankle-brachial index for screening asymptomatic PAD in diabetic patients over 50 with risk factors

Foot ulcer workup: probe-to-bone testing with a blunt sterile instrument, plain radiographs for osteomyelitis in chronic non-healing ulcers, MRI (most specific) with nuclear/labeled-WBC studies as alternatives; cultures from debrided ulcer base or purulent aspirate
Cardiac stress testing in diabetic patients with symptoms (even atypical) suggestive of ischemia (routine screening of asymptomatic patients is not recommended)
redFlags: Neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, or traction involving the macula - urgent panretinal laser photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF; surgical vitrectomy for severe proliferative disease with vitreous hemorrhage
Foot wound that probes to bone (high likelihood of osteomyelitis) or rapidly spreading cellulitis/severe infection requiring IV broad-spectrum coverage and possible surgical debridement

Severe infections seen largely in diabetes: rhinocerebral mucormycosis, malignant (invasive) otitis externa progressing to osteomyelitis/meningitis, emphysematous pyelonephritis/cystitis/cholecystitis - consider especially with severe hyperglycemia

Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy with resting tachycardia, reduced heart-rate variability, orthostatic hypotension, and QTc prolongation - associated with silent ischemia and reports of sudden death
Hypoglycemia unawareness from autonomic neuropathy/reduced counterregulation, increasing the risk of severe hypoglycemia
Hyperkalemia/acidemia from type IV RTA, potentially exacerbated by ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists
Risk of radiocontrast-induced nephrotoxicity (preexisting nephropathy, volume depletion)
harrison.prognosis: Complications account for most diabetes-related morbidity and mortality. Diagnosis at a younger age increases lifetime complication burden (one estimate: 3-4 fewer years of life expectancy per decade of earlier diagnosis). Intensive glycemic control substantially improves outcomes: DCCT projections estimated several additional years free of vision loss, end-stage renal disease, and amputation, with overall added life expectancy, and 30-year follow-up showed durable reductions in retinopathy, nephropathy, and cardiovascular events (legacy/metabolic-memory effect). About 20-40% of patients develop diabetic nephropathy, and CKD on dialysis carries a poor prognosis. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death and outcomes after CHD are worse than in nondiabetic patients; CHD tends to involve multiple vessels and revascularization (PCI/CABG) is less durable, though CABG plus optimal medical therapy generally outperforms PCI. Diabetic polyradiculopathies (including amyotrophy) are usually self-limited, resolving over 6-12 months. Foot ulcers carry a substantial amputation risk (about 14-24% with that or subsequent ulceration). Some patients never develop retinopathy or nephropathy despite long-standing disease, suggesting genetic protection.
pitfalls: Routine urinalysis does not detect low-level albuminuria - use UACR; and some patients lose GFR without albuminuria, so always assess both eGFR and UACR
Nondilated eye exams by primary providers miss diabetic eye disease - a dilated/photographic retinal exam is required
Once advanced retinopathy or moderate albuminuria is established, improving glycemic control provides less benefit - early detection is critical
Diagnosing diabetic neuropathy without excluding other etiologies; metformin can lower vitamin B12 and pernicious anemia is more common in type 1 disease
Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria unnecessarily; basing diabetic foot infection diagnosis on superficial swab cultures rather than clinical judgment and deep cultures

Failure to hold metformin around iodinated contrast and to monitor creatinine 24-48 h afterward; failing to reassess glucose-lowering drug choice/dose as GFR falls (sulfonylureas and metformin contraindicated in advanced renal insufficiency; SGLT-2 inhibitors ineffective below eGFR 20)
Overlooking silent ischemia given frequent absence of chest pain, and failing to evaluate before major surgery
harrison.severityClassification: Retinopathy: nonproliferative (mild to severe, with microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA) versus proliferative (neovascularization), with clinically significant macular edema as a separate sight-threatening category. Albuminuria/CKD: UACR normal (<30 mg/g), moderately increased (30-299 mg/g), severely increased (>300 mg/g), staged alongside eGFR; nephrology referral when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, UACR >300 mg/g, or atypical features (hematuria, rapid decline). Diabetic neuropathy categorized as diffuse (distal symmetric polyneuropathy and/or autonomic), focal mononeuropathy, or radiculopathy/polyradiculopathy. Foot infection severity stratified clinically from mild/non-limb-threatening (oral antibiotics) to severe (IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, offloading, debridement).
management: Optimise glycaemic control early to reduce microvascular complications, harnessing the durable legacy or metabolic-memory benefit of sustained control
Retinopathy: panretinal laser photocoagulation for proliferative disease and intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for macular oedema
Nephropathy: renin-angiotensin blockade with an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus SGLT2 inhibitors, alongside blood-pressure and albuminuria control
Neuropathy: protective foot care, neuropathic-pain agents and management of autonomic features such as gastroparesis
Diabetic foot: offloading, debridement, antimicrobials for infection, revascularisation and a multidisciplinary foot service
Macrovascular risk reduction with statins, antihypertensives, antiplatelet therapy where indicated and smoking cessation
Structured surveillance with dilated retinal examination, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio with eGFR, and monofilament and vibration foot screening
Escalate to ophthalmology, nephrology or vascular specialists for progressive complications
